wb2_rule.topic: Jordanian rule of the West Bank

claims.text: A 1949 amendment to the Nationality Law effectively imposed Jordanian citizenship on local Palestinians and refugees; the West and East Banks each received 30 seats in parliament; in 1953 Hussein called East Jerusalem the 'alternative capital'; Israelis were barred from the Old City and holy sites and the access committee never formed; Jordan expelled the Jewish residents of East Jerusalem and much of the Jewish Quarter including the Hurva Synagogue was destroyed; the UK recognized the union excluding Jerusalem, Iraq also recognized it, Pakistan's recognition is disputed; in May 1950 the Arab League Political Committee found the annexation illegal and in June treated Jordan as holding the territory in 'trust'; on 31 July 1988 Hussein severed legal and administrative ties with the West Bank.

Jordan's 1954 Nationality Law granted citizenship to 'any person who, not being Jewish, possessed Palestinian nationality before 15 May 1948' and resided ordinarily in the kingdom; unlike other Arab host states Jordan extended citizenship to West Bank residents and refugees.

At Samu on 13 November 1966 Israel said it was retaliating for a mine, reportedly laid by Fatah, that killed three soldiers; the UN put houses destroyed at 125, the IDF at 40; 16 Jordanian soldiers and airmen and 3 civilians were killed and one Israeli colonel; riots spread across the West Bank demanding Hussein's overthrow and Jordanian police killed four Palestinians.
